articles.body_html:
Pipedream Workflows and String stop running on March 31, 2027. All Workflows data, including connected accounts and their OAuth tokens, is deleted by April 30, 2027. Pipedream Connect is not affected.

Neither Pipedream nor n8n offers an importer, so moving to n8n means rebuilding each workflow in n8n's own format. Most of it is mechanical once you know the equivalents. This post covers the equivalents, the parts that break, and an order of work.

1. Get your workflows out

You have three ways to get workflow definitions:

  • The official export. In a project, open Settings and click Export Workflows. Pipedream writes a ZIP to the project's File Store: a manifest.json plus one JSON file per workflow, with triggers, steps, code, props and branches. Pipedream's docs say File Stores are an Advanced-plan feature, so on Free or Basic the button may not work.
  • GitHub Sync. If a project was ever synced, the repository has a workflow.yaml per workflow and a file per code step.
  • The REST API. GET https://api.pipedream.com/v1/workflows/{id}?org_id=o_xxx with an API key returns a workflow's definition. It isn't confirmed on Free or Basic plans, so try one workflow first.

Whatever you use, some things never come out:

  • secret values, which are exported as <redacted>;
  • OAuth tokens, which become just an account ID;
  • environment variable values;
  • data store records and File Store files;
  • event history;
  • the code of private components.

Read manifest.json first: its warnings list names every redacted prop. One export holds at most 500 workflows or 256 MB.

Save a few real sample events from each workflow now. On Free and Basic, Pipedream keeps only the last 100 events or 7 days. You'll want them to test the n8n version.

2. Choose n8n Cloud or self-hosted

This choice depends mostly on your code steps:

  • n8n Cloud. The Code node can load only crypto and moment in JavaScript. Python steps can't import anything at all.
  • Self-hosted n8n. Set NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_EXTERNAL=axios,lodash (and NODE_FUNCTION_ALLOW_BUILTIN for Node's own modules), and install the packages where the task runner can load them.

If most of your imports are HTTP clients and date libraries, Cloud is fine: HTTP calls can use this.helpers.httpRequest() inside the Code node, and Luxon is built in. If you depend on SDKs or Python libraries, self-hosting saves a lot of rewriting.

3. Map the triggers

Pipedream n8n
HTTP / webhook trigger Webhook node
$.respond() in a step Respond to Webhook node, with the Webhook node's Respond option set to "Using 'Respond to Webhook' Node"
Schedule (cron or interval) Schedule Trigger
App event (new row, new email…) The app's n8n trigger node, if it exists

Three things bite here:

  • Webhook URLs change. Every service that calls your *.m.pipedream.net URL needs the new n8n production URL.
  • Some intervals don't fit one rule. n8n's interval rules count seconds up to 59, minutes up to 59, hours up to 23 and days up to 31. "Every 90 minutes" becomes two cron rules: 0 0,3,6,9,12,15,18,21 * * * and 30 1,4,7,10,13,16,19,22 * * *.
  • Polling triggers batch items. Pipedream ran your workflow once per new row or email. n8n's polling triggers (Google Sheets, Gmail, Airtable…) return every new item in one execution. Code written for a single event quietly processes only the first one. Either put Loop Over Items after the trigger and call the rest of the flow with Execute Workflow per item, or rewrite the code for $input.all().

4. Map steps and branches

Pipedream n8n
Registry action (Slack, Google Sheets…) The app's n8n node, or HTTP Request
If/else block If node (one condition branch) or Switch node (several)
Switch block Switch node in Rules mode
Filter step, $.flow.exit() If node with nothing connected to the branch that stops
Delay Wait node
Parallel block Branches from one node, then a Merge node
Loop block Loop Over Items

One difference changes results silently: Pipedream's rule builder compares text without regard to case, and n8n's If node is case-sensitive unless you turn on its Ignore Case option.

Steps after a Pipedream block read steps.<block>.$return_value, the result of whichever branch ran. In n8n, add a node where the branches meet and point later expressions at it.

Prop expressions change syntax too: {{steps.trigger.event.body.email}} becomes {{ $('trigger').first().json.body.email }}. Name your n8n nodes after the old step names and most references translate one to one.

5. Convert the code steps

A Pipedream Node.js step:

import axios from "axios";

export default defineComponent({
  async run({ steps, $ }) {
    const email = steps.trigger.event.body.email;
    const { data } = await axios.get("https://api.example.com/users", { params: { email } });
    if (!data.active) return $.flow.exit("inactive user");
    $.export("userId", data.id);
    return data;
  },
});

The same logic in an n8n Code node ("Run Once for All Items", with the Webhook node named trigger):

const email = $('trigger').first().json.body.email;
const data = await this.helpers.httpRequest({
  method: 'GET',
  url: 'https://api.example.com/users',
  qs: { email },
  json: true,
});

// Like $.flow.exit(): no items out, so nothing after this node runs.
if (!data.active) return [];

return [{ json: { ...data, userId: data.id } }];

The rules behind it:

  • steps.x.$return_value becomes $('x').first().json.
  • $.export() and the return value become fields of the items you return. n8n items are always objects, so wrap a string or an array.
  • $.flow.exit() becomes return [].
  • axios, got and node-fetch become this.helpers.httpRequest(), which works on n8n Cloud.
  • Pipedream data stores become workflow static data ($getWorkflowStaticData('global')) or n8n Data tables. Static data is only saved for published workflows started by a trigger, not for manual test runs.
  • Code nodes can't read n8n credentials by design. If a step used this.someApp.$auth, move that API call into an HTTP Request node that uses an n8n credential.

6. Credentials, secrets and variables

  1. Create an n8n credential for every connected account and select it on the matching nodes.
  2. Re-enter redacted secrets in credentials, or as n8n Variables. Variables are available on n8n Cloud Pro and Enterprise and on self-hosted Business and Enterprise.
  3. Since n8n 2.0, N8N_BLOCK_ENV_ACCESS_IN_NODE defaults to true, so Code nodes can't read environment variables unless you change it on a self-hosted instance.

7. Import, test and cut over

  1. Import each workflow JSON from the editor (workflow menu, Import from File), or in bulk with the public API: POST /api/v1/workflows with an X-N8N-API-KEY header. The API isn't available on the Cloud free trial.
  2. Imported workflows start unpublished. In n8n 2.x you publish a workflow instead of toggling it active.
  3. Replay your saved sample events and compare the outputs with Pipedream's.
  4. Point each webhook sender at the new production URL. Watch the Executions list for a few days, then turn the Pipedream workflow off.
  5. Copy data store records and File Store files out before April 30, 2027.

Start with the workflows that have the most outside dependencies (webhook senders, OAuth apps), because those take the longest to switch. If you're stuck on a specific Pipedream pattern, ask in the comments.

This article was written with the help of AI. The mappings and the code example were checked against Pipedream workflows converted and run in n8n 2.x.

articles.title: From Buggy Prototype to Polished Arcade: How I Upgraded Three Browser Games
articles.description: From Buggy Prototype to Polished Arcade: How I Upgraded Three Browser Games   Over the past...
articles.body_html:
From Buggy Prototype to Polished Arcade: How I Upgraded Three Browser Games

Over the past few days I've been deep in the trenches refactoring and rebuilding three browser games built on a lightweight 2D/3D canvas engine. What started as "fix a few bugs" turned into a full-blown feature overhaul across a platformer, a racer, and an FPS.

Here's what actually changed, why, and what I learned.

The Starting Point

Three games, all built on the same homegrown engine:

  • Neon Caverns: Seasons — a platformer with 20 levels and a coin economy
  • Death Boost: Seasons — a pseudo-3D arcade racer
  • Riftfire (formerly Raycast FPS) — a raycast shooter

The initial request was simple: "there are bugs." But as I dug in, the real issues were architectural — not just a few typos.

Neon Caverns: Seasons

The Bugs

Two silent killers were ruining the game:

1. Tile mutations across restarts. The engine's tilemap constructor mutated a shared array every time a level loaded. After one restart, every tile lookup broke. Players saw invisible walls.

2. The pause button drifted off screen. It was added as a world-space entity, so it scrolled away with the camera instead of staying pinned to the HUD.

The Overhaul

  • 4 seasons × 12 levels = 48 unique stages, each procedurally generated but deterministic per run.
  • Ramping difficulty curve — enemy HP, speed, accuracy, and map density all scale with a single normalized value from 0 to 1.
  • Full procedural audio — every sound effect and music track is synthesized live via the Web Audio API. No external files, no downloads.
  • Persistent coins and upgrades — health, speed, jump, magnet range, shield tiers, all saved to localStorage.
  • Star ratings per level (1–3 stars based on health, time, and coin collection).
  • Season unlock chaining — clear all 12 levels of a season to open the next one.

Death Boost: Seasons

The Bugs

This game had a list:

  • Invisible hazards were killing players
  • Cars were colliding from behind the player
  • Traffic recycled to a moving target, causing pile-ups
  • Menu clicks silently failed when audio init threw
  • Sprites rendered ~1000× too small to be visible

The Overhaul

  • 4× wider road — from 2000 to 3400 units wide, 5 lanes instead of 3.
  • 60% fewer obstacles, 50% less traffic, longer spacing between hazards.
  • 12 tracks total with lap counts from 1 to 3.
  • Bug fixes: signed z-window for hazard collisions, cooldowns on repeated hits, sprite scale corrected to match world geometry, audio failures no longer swallow input.
  • Always-visible pause button — now pinned to screen coordinates instead of world space.
  • Per-level difficulty display — cars show their speed, health, and boost stats as animated bars.

Riftfire

The Overhaul

What was originally a 5-map raycast FPS became:

  • 12 seasons × 30 levels = 360 stages, all procedurally generated with seeded randomness.
  • Difficulty ramp — enemy HP, damage, accuracy, speed, and fire rate all scale from easy (level 1) to brutal (level 360).
  • Procedural audio — every gunshot has its own synthesized waveform. Rifle, pistol, shotgun, sniper, minigun — all distinct, all generated at runtime.
  • Adaptive music — four different musical scales that switch based on the current level's difficulty.
  • Weapons shop, ranks, and coin economy — buy new weapons, earn XP, climb 10 ranks.
  • Mobile touch support — analog joystick for movement, drag-to-aim for firing.

The Common Threads

Across all three games, the same principles showed up again and again:

1. Separate World Space from Screen Space

The pause button bug and the sprite scale bug both came from mixing world coordinates with screen coordinates. Anything that should stay fixed on the HUD must be drawn after the camera transform is popped.

2. Never Trust Global Mutable State

The tilemap bug was caused by an engine-level array.unshift() that silently mutated data shared between level loads. Whenever possible, rebuild state fresh at scene boundaries.

3. Procedural Content Is Cheap and Endless

All three games now generate their content at runtime. This means:

  • No asset loading delays
  • No missing-file errors
  • No copyright issues
  • No download size

Web Audio can synthesize a gunshot, a jump sound, or a full musical theme in a few lines of code.

4. Input Handling Must Be Defensive

The click-swallowing bug in Death Boost happened because initAudio() threw an exception and aborted the event listener before pendingClick was ever set. Always set state before calling anything that might throw.

5. Difficulty Should Be a Single Scalar

Rather than tweaking 20 numbers per level, each game derives all difficulty factors from one normalized value:

difficulty = (globalLevel / totalLevels) ^ 0.85

That one number then scales enemy HP, count, speed, accuracy, and map density. It's clean, tunable, and easy to reason about.

What I'd Do Differently

If I started over:

  1. Version control from day one. This was all done in single monolithic files.
  2. Write tests for input flow. The click bug was caught by a human, not a test.
  3. Separate rendering from state. Several bugs came from render functions that also mutated game state.
  4. Build a small dev console — a way to jump to any level, tweak difficulty, and inspect state.

Final Numbers

Game Levels Audio Notable Feature
Neon Caverns: Seasons 48 100% procedural Season unlock chains
Death Boost: Seasons 12 tracks 100% procedural Multi-lap enduros
Riftfire 360 100% procedural Adaptive music scales

All three ship as single HTML files, no external assets, and run in any modern browser.

Closing Thoughts

The best thing about browser games is how fast the iteration loop can be. Change a number, refresh the page, feel the difference. The worst thing is how quickly small architectural mistakes compound into invisible bugs.

The three games above went from "playable but broken" to "actually fun" by fixing a handful of fundamental issues and then building outward. Every new feature is now cheap to add because the foundation is solid.

If you're building a browser game and something feels off, it's almost never "just one bug." It's usually a small design decision that ignored a boundary between two systems. Find the boundary. Fix the boundary. The rest follows.

articles.title: An 11-Week React Roadmap: What to Build Before 2026 Ends
articles.description: A week-by-week React plan from Oct 14 to Dec 31: TypeScript, React 19, Next.js, data, design systems, testing and AI, with a project at every stop.
articles.body_html:
Most "learn React" plans fail for the same reason: they're lists of topics with no dates and nothing to ship.

So here's a different format. The calendar says there are about 11 weeks left in 2026, and that's enough time to go from "I know some React" to "I have a deployed full-stack app, a tested design system, an AI feature and a portfolio with case studies."

This is a plan in 7 stops, each with a date range, a checklist and one thing you must build before moving on.

A note before we start: this is an ambitious, opinionated plan, and it assumes you already know basic React (components, props, state). If you can only spare a few hours a week, don't skip stops. Cut the scope inside each one. There's a section on that near the end.

The plan at a glance

Stop Dates Focus You ship
01 Oct 14 – 20 Foundations One mini-UI with modern CSS only
02 Oct 21 – Nov 3 React 19 deep dive A small React 19 form app
03 Nov 4 – 17 Full-stack Next.js A deployed CRUD app with auth
04 Nov 18 – 24 State, data and forms A typed data layer with live updates
05 Nov 25 – Dec 8 UI and design system 10 documented, accessible components
06 Dec 9 – 18 Test, speed and CI E2E tests, a CI pipeline, error monitoring
07 Dec 19 – 31 AI feature and ship A streaming AI UI and a published portfolio

The order is deliberate. Each stop produces something the next one needs: the form app from stop 2 becomes the starting point for stop 3, the components from stop 5 get tested in stop 6, and so on.

Stop 1 (Oct 14 – 20): Lock the foundations

The checklist

  • Audit your gaps in JS, TypeScript and modern CSS
  • TypeScript strict mode: generics, narrowing, utility types
  • CSS nesting, @layer, container queries
  • Build one mini-UI with modern CSS only
  • Set up pnpm, ESLint, Prettier and Husky

One week is short, so don't try to "learn TypeScript." Instead, find your gaps. Open a few components you've written and ask where you used any, where you cast with as, and where you copied a type without understanding it.

TypeScript: the three ideas that pay off in React

Generics show up the moment you write a reusable component or hook:

function useLocalStorage<T>(key: string, initial: T) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(() => {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
    return raw ? (JSON.parse(raw) as T) : initial;
  });
  // ...
  return [value, setValue] as const;
}

Narrowing is how you handle API results safely:

type Result =
  | { status: "success"; data: User }
  | { status: "error"; message: string };

function render(result: Result) {
  if (result.status === "error") return result.message; // narrowed here
  return result.data.name;                               // and here
}

Utility types (Pick, Omit, Partial, ReturnType) save you from retyping the same shape:

type UserPreview = Pick<User, "id" | "name" | "avatarUrl">;
type UserDraft = Partial<Omit<User, "id">>;

Turn on "strict": true in tsconfig.json if you haven't. It's uncomfortable for a day and valuable afterward.

Modern CSS you can use today

Native nesting, cascade layers and container queries remove a lot of reasons to reach for a preprocessor or a utility framework for small components:

@layer base, components;

@layer components {
  .card-wrapper {
    container-type: inline-size;
  }

  .card {
    padding: 1rem;
    border-radius: 0.75rem;

    & h3 {
      margin: 0;
    }

    @container (min-width: 480px) {
      display: grid;
      grid-template-columns: 160px 1fr;
      gap: 1rem;
    }
  }
}

The project for this stop is one mini-UI using only modern CSS: a pricing card, a profile card or a dashboard tile. No Tailwind, no component library. The point is to find out what you can do without them.

Tooling

Set up the boring stuff now so it doesn't interrupt you later:

pnpm create vite my-app --template react-ts
cd my-app
pnpm add -D eslint prettier husky lint-staged
pnpm exec husky init

A pre-commit hook that runs lint and format on staged files will catch most embarrassing commits before your teammates (or recruiters) see them.

Done when: strict TS compiles cleanly, your mini-UI works at three container widths, and committing triggers lint and format.

Stop 2 (Oct 21 – Nov 3): React 19 deep dive

The checklist

  • Actions, useActionState, useOptimistic
  • The use() hook and Suspense data loading
  • Enable React Compiler in one project
  • Refactor an old app: drop memo clutter
  • Ship a small React 19 form app

This stop gets two weeks because it changes how you write React day to day.

Actions and useActionState

Before React 19, a form that submits to an API meant hand-rolling isLoading, error and data state. Now an async function can be the form's action, and React tracks the pending state for you:

import { useActionState } from "react";

type State = { ok: boolean; message: string } | null;

async function subscribe(_prev: State, formData: FormData): Promise<State> {
  const email = String(formData.get("email") ?? "");
  const res = await fetch("/api/subscribe", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ email }),
  });
  return res.ok
    ? { ok: true, message: "Subscribed!" }
    : { ok: false, message: "Something went wrong" };
}

export function Newsletter() {
  const [state, action, isPending] = useActionState(subscribe, null);

  return (
    <form action={action}>
      <input name="email" type="email" required />
      <button disabled={isPending}>
        {isPending ? "Subscribing..." : "Subscribe"}
      </button>
      {state && <p role="status">{state.message}</p>}
    </form>
  );
}

useOptimistic

Optimistic UI means showing the result before the server confirms it. useOptimistic gives you a temporary value that automatically reverts to the real state when the action finishes:

import { useOptimistic } from "react";

function TodoList({ todos, addTodo }: Props) {
  const [optimisticTodos, addOptimistic] = useOptimistic(
    todos,
    (current, newTitle: string) => [
      ...current,
      { id: crypto.randomUUID(), title: newTitle, pending: true },
    ]
  );

  async function formAction(formData: FormData) {
    const title = String(formData.get("title"));
    addOptimistic(title);
    await addTodo(title); // if this throws, the optimistic item disappears
  }

  return (
    <form action={formAction}>
      <input name="title" />
      <ul>
        {optimisticTodos.map((t) => (
          <li key={t.id} style={{ opacity: t.pending ? 0.5 : 1 }}>
            {t.title}
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>
    </form>
  );
}

use() and Suspense

use() reads a promise (or context) during render and suspends until it resolves. The important rule: the promise must be stable across renders. Creating a new fetch() inside the component body creates a new promise every render. Pass it down from a parent, a framework loader, or a cache:

import { use, Suspense } from "react";

function Comments({ commentsPromise }: { commentsPromise: Promise<Comment[]> }) {
  const comments = use(commentsPromise);
  return comments.map((c) => <p key={c.id}>{c.text}</p>);
}

export function Post({ commentsPromise }: Props) {
  return (
    <Suspense fallback={<p>Loading comments...</p>}>
      <Comments commentsPromise={commentsPromise} />
    </Suspense>
  );
}

React Compiler and the memo cleanup

The React Compiler memoizes components and values at build time. If you've sprinkled useMemo, useCallback and React.memo through a codebase "just in case," the compiler makes most of it unnecessary.

With Vite it's a Babel plugin:

pnpm add -D babel-plugin-react-compiler

// vite.config.js
import { defineConfig } from "vite";
import react from "@vitejs/plugin-react";

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [
    react({
      babel: { plugins: ["babel-plugin-react-compiler"] },
    }),
  ],
});

Setup differs by framework and version, so follow the official React Compiler docs for yours.

The refactor exercise from the roadmap is the best part of this stop:

  1. Pick an old project with lots of manual memoization
  2. Profile it with React DevTools before changing anything
  3. Enable the compiler
  4. Remove manual memoization in small batches
  5. Profile again and compare

Remove useMemo/useCallback where it's only there for performance. Keep it where a value's identity genuinely matters (for example a dependency of an effect that shouldn't re-run). And measure. Don't assume.

Done when: you've shipped a small form app using actions and optimistic updates, and you can explain why you kept or removed each manual memo.

Stop 3 (Nov 4 – 17): Full-stack Next.js

The checklist

  • Server Components and Server Functions
  • CRUD app: Next.js + Postgres/Prisma
  • Auth with Auth.js or Clerk, plus middleware
  • Streaming, caching and revalidation
  • Deploy on Vercel with preview URLs

This is the biggest conceptual jump in the plan. Give it the time.

Server Components: data fetching without an API layer

A Server Component runs on the server, so it can talk to the database directly. Nothing from it ships to the browser except the rendered output:

// app/posts/page.tsx (Server Component by default)
import { prisma } from "@/lib/prisma";

export default async function PostsPage() {
  const posts = await prisma.post.findMany({
    orderBy: { createdAt: "desc" },
  });

  return (
    <ul>
      {posts.map((p) => (
        <li key={p.id}>{p.title}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

Server Functions for mutations 

// app/posts/actions.ts
"use server";

import { revalidatePath } from "next/cache";
import { z } from "zod";
import { prisma } from "@/lib/prisma";
import { auth } from "@/lib/auth";

const Schema = z.object({ title: z.string().min(1).max(120) });

export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
  const session = await auth();
  if (!session) throw new Error("Unauthorized");

  const parsed = Schema.safeParse({ title: formData.get("title") });
  if (!parsed.success) return { error: "Invalid title" };

  await prisma.post.create({
    data: { title: parsed.data.title, authorId: session.user.id },
  });
  revalidatePath("/posts");
}

Treat every Server Function like a public HTTP endpoint, because that's what it is. It needs its own authentication check and input validation. Hiding a button in the UI is not authorization. This is one of the most common mistakes in this model, and the roadmap's "auth + middleware" item exists partly to drive the point home.

Auth

Both Auth.js and Clerk are reasonable. A rough rule: Auth.js if you want to own the data and the flow, Clerk if you'd rather not build sign-in, sessions and user management yourself. Whichever you pick, use middleware (called proxy in newer Next.js versions, so check your version's docs) for coarse route protection, and still verify the session inside your data access code.

Streaming, caching and revalidation

Three questions to answer for every page:

  1. Can the shell render immediately? Use loading.tsx or <Suspense> so slow data doesn't block the whole page.
  2. How fresh does this data need to be? Per-user data usually shouldn't be cached shared. A blog list can be.
  3. What invalidates it? Tie mutations to revalidatePath or tag-based revalidation.

Caching defaults have changed between Next.js versions, so don't rely on tutorials older than your installed version. Read the current caching docs, then test by actually mutating data and watching what updates.

Deploy early

Push to GitHub, connect to Vercel, and every pull request gets a preview URL. Do this on day one of this stop, not day fourteen. Deploy problems are easier to fix when the app is tiny.

Done when: you have a deployed CRUD app with sign-in, where logged-out users can't mutate data even if they call the Server Function directly.

Stop 4 (Nov 18 – 24): State, data and forms

The checklist

  • TanStack Query: cache, mutations, prefetch
  • Zustand or Redux Toolkit for UI state
  • React Hook Form + Zod validation
  • Typed API layer: tRPC or OpenAPI
  • Live updates via SSE / WebSockets

One week, so focus on the mental model: server state and client state are different things.

State type Examples Tool
Server state Lists, profiles, anything from an API TanStack Query (or your framework's data layer)
Client UI state Open modal, selected tab, filters useState, then Zustand or Redux Toolkit if shared widely
Form state Inputs, errors, dirty/touched React Hook Form
Validation Shape and rules of data Zod

TanStack Query: cache and mutations 

import { useQuery, useMutation, useQueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";

function Todos() {
  const queryClient = useQueryClient();

  const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["todos"],
    queryFn: () => fetch("/api/todos").then((r) => r.json()),
  });

  const addTodo = useMutation({
    mutationFn: (title: string) =>
      fetch("/api/todos", {
        method: "POST",
        body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
      }),
    onSuccess: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["todos"] }),
  });

  if (isPending) return <p>Loading...</p>;
  if (error) return <p>Something went wrong</p>;
  // render data, call addTodo.mutate(...)
}

Spend time on queryKey design and invalidation. Most TanStack Query bugs are cache-key bugs.

Forms: React Hook Form + Zod

Define the schema once, then use it for both types and validation:

import { useForm } from "react-hook-form";
import { zodResolver } from "@hookform/resolvers/zod";
import { z } from "zod";

const Schema = z.object({
  email: z.string().email("Enter a valid email"),
  age: z.coerce.number().int().min(18, "Must be 18 or older"),
});
type FormValues = z.infer<typeof Schema>;

export function SignupForm() {
  const {
    register,
    handleSubmit,
    formState: { errors, isSubmitting },
  } = useForm<FormValues>({ resolver: zodResolver(Schema) });

  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(async (values) => { /* send */ })}>
      <input {...register("email")} />
      {errors.email && <p role="alert">{errors.email.message}</p>}
      <input type="number" {...register("age")} />
      {errors.age && <p role="alert">{errors.age.message}</p>}
      <button disabled={isSubmitting}>Sign up</button>
    </form>
  );
}

Remember that client-side validation is for UX. The server must validate again with the same schema.

Typed API layer

  • tRPC gives end-to-end type safety with no schema file, but works best when your frontend and backend are both TypeScript and in the same repo or workspace.
  • OpenAPI with a generated client is a better fit when the backend is a different language or owned by another team.

Pick whichever matches your situation, and try the other briefly so you know the trade-off.

Live updates

For one-way updates (notifications, progress, a live feed), Server-Sent Events are simpler than WebSockets:

useEffect(() => {
  const source = new EventSource("/api/notifications");
  source.onmessage = (e) => {
    const event = JSON.parse(e.data);
    queryClient.setQueryData(["notifications"], (old = []) => [event, ...old]);
  };
  return () => source.close();
}, [queryClient]);

Use WebSockets when you need two-way, low-latency communication such as chat or collaborative editing.

Done when: your app from stop 3 has a typed data layer, a validated form, and at least one feature that updates live without a refresh.

Stop 5 (Nov 25 – Dec 8): UI and design system

The checklist

  • Tailwind v4 + design tokens
  • 10 components with Radix / shadcn/ui
  • Document them in Storybook
  • Pass an axe audit: keyboard, ARIA, contrast
  • Dark mode, motion and i18n

Design tokens in Tailwind v4

Tailwind v4 moved configuration into CSS. Your tokens live in @theme:

@import "tailwindcss";

@theme {
  --color-brand-500: oklch(0.62 0.19 259);
  --color-surface: oklch(0.99 0 0);
  --radius-card: 0.75rem;
  --font-sans: "Inter", system-ui, sans-serif;
}

Then bg-brand-500 and rounded-card just work. The benefit of tokens is that a rebrand or a dark theme becomes a change in one file.

Ten components, not fifty

Pick ten you'd genuinely reuse: Button, Input, Select, Checkbox, Dialog, Dropdown menu, Tabs, Toast, Card, Skeleton. Build them on Radix primitives or copy them in via shadcn/ui and then actually read and adjust the code. The value of shadcn/ui is that you own the components, so treat them as your code.

Storybook as documentation

For each component, write stories for its meaningful states: default, disabled, loading, error, long text and dark mode. If you can't think of a state to document, you probably don't understand the component's contract yet.

Accessibility audit

Run the audit in this order:

  1. Keyboard only: unplug the mouse. Can you reach and operate everything? Is focus visible? Does a dialog trap and restore focus?
  2. Automated: run axe (the browser extension, @axe-core/playwright, or Storybook's a11y addon). It finds a portion of issues, not all.
  3. Contrast: check text and UI against WCAG AA ratios.
  4. Screen reader spot check: at least try VoiceOver or NVDA on one flow.

Dark mode, motion and i18n 

@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  * {
    animation-duration: 0.01ms !important;
    transition-duration: 0.01ms !important;
  }
}

Respect prefers-color-scheme and prefers-reduced-motion by default, and use a library such as next-intl or react-i18next to pull strings out of components early. Retrofitting i18n into a finished UI is painful.

Done when: you have ten documented components that pass keyboard navigation and an axe scan, in both light and dark themes.

Stop 6 (Dec 9 – 18): Test, speed and CI

The checklist

  • Vitest + React Testing Library for core flows
  • Playwright E2E for 3 user journeys
  • INP under 200ms, LCP under 2.5s
  • GitHub Actions: lint, test, deploy
  • Sentry error monitoring

Unit and component tests

Test what the user experiences, not implementation details:

import { render, screen } from "@testing-library/react";
import userEvent from "@testing-library/user-event";
import { SignupForm } from "./SignupForm";

test("shows a validation error for an invalid email", async () => {
  const user = userEvent.setup();
  render(<SignupForm />);

  await user.type(screen.getByRole("textbox", { name: /email/i }), "nope");
  await user.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /sign up/i }));

  expect(await screen.findByRole("alert")).toHaveTextContent(/valid email/i);
});

Selecting by role and accessible name pushes you toward accessible markup as a side effect.

Three E2E journeys

Don't try to cover everything. Pick the three flows that would hurt most if they broke, for example sign in, create a post, and checkout (or whatever your app's core action is):

import { test, expect } from "@playwright/test";

test("signed-in user can create a post", async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto("/login");
  await page.getByLabel("Email").fill("test@example.com");
  await page.getByLabel("Password").fill(process.env.E2E_PASSWORD!);
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Sign in" }).click();

  await page.getByRole("link", { name: "New post" }).click();
  await page.getByLabel("Title").fill("Hello from Playwright");
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Publish" }).click();

  await expect(page.getByText("Hello from Playwright")).toBeVisible();
});

Performance targets

The roadmap's targets match Google's "good" thresholds for Core Web Vitals: LCP at or under 2.5 seconds and INP under 200 milliseconds (at the 75th percentile of real users). A few notes:

  • Lighthouse gives you lab data. It's useful for debugging but not the same as what your users experience.
  • INP measures responsiveness across the whole visit, so it's usually hurt by long tasks from heavy JavaScript. Look at the Performance panel for long tasks after interactions.
  • LCP is most often an image or hero text problem. Check what the LCP element actually is before optimizing anything.

You can capture field data from your own app with the web-vitals library:

import { onINP, onLCP } from "web-vitals";

onINP((metric) => console.log("INP", metric.value));
onLCP((metric) => console.log("LCP", metric.value));

CI with GitHub Actions 

name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  check:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pnpm/action-setup@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 22
          cache: pnpm
      - run: pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
      - run: pnpm lint
      - run: pnpm tsc --noEmit
      - run: pnpm test run

Action and Node versions move over time, so check the current ones when you copy this. Add the Playwright job after the basics work.

Error monitoring

Add Sentry (or an equivalent) and deliberately trigger a test error in production. The first time you see a real stack trace with source maps is when monitoring clicks.

Done when: a pull request that breaks a core flow fails CI, and an error in production shows up in your monitoring tool.

Stop 7 (Dec 19 – 31): AI feature and ship

The checklist

  • Streaming AI chat UI with Vercel AI SDK
  • Try tool-calling and MCP in an app
  • Publish portfolio with 3 case studies
  • Write on DEV.to and post an X thread
  • Plan 2027: pick 1 deep-dive track

Build the AI feature with the right expectations

Most of the engineering in an AI feature is UX, not the model call. A server route that streams a response looks roughly like this with the Vercel AI SDK:

// app/api/chat/route.ts
import { streamText, convertToModelMessages, type UIMessage } from "ai";

export async function POST(req: Request) {
  const { messages }: { messages: UIMessage[] } = await req.json();

  const result = streamText({
    model: "YOUR_MODEL_ID", // see the SDK docs for supported models
    messages: convertToModelMessages(messages),
  });

  return result.toUIMessageStreamResponse();
}

The SDK's API has changed between major versions, so follow the docs for the version you install rather than copying older examples.

The frontend questions that actually matter:

  • What does the user see while the model is thinking?
  • What happens when a response is wrong, slow or fails halfway?
  • Can the user stop a response, retry, or edit their message?
  • Where does it stop being trustworthy, and is that visible to the user?

Treat model output as untrusted input. Don't render it as raw HTML, and don't let it call tools with side effects (sending email, deleting data) without validation and user confirmation.

Tool-calling and MCP

Tool-calling lets the model request that your code run a function with structured arguments, such as "look up this order" or "search these docs." MCP (Model Context Protocol) standardizes how apps expose tools and data to models. For this stop, one small experiment is enough: give your app a read-only tool and watch how the model decides when to use it. Keep write actions behind explicit confirmation.

Ship the portfolio and write about it

This is the step people skip, and it's the one that makes the other six count.

A case study doesn't need to be long. For each of three projects, cover:

  1. The problem: what it does and who it's for
  2. A decision you made: and what you rejected
  3. Something that went wrong: and how you found the cause
  4. What you'd change: being honest builds more trust than being polished

Then write about it on DEV.to, post a short X thread, and link the repo and live demo. Use only results you actually measured. Don't claim a Lighthouse score or a speedup you didn't verify.

Plan 2027

Finish with a decision: pick one deep-dive track for the new year, such as performance, design systems, full-stack architecture, testing, or AI engineering. Breadth got you through this plan. Depth is what makes you recognizable.

Done when: your portfolio is live with three case studies, you've published at least one write-up, and you can say in one sentence what you're going deeper on next.

Common mistakes with a plan like this

  • Tutorial hopping instead of building. Every stop has a deliverable for a reason. If you haven't shipped something, you haven't finished the stop.
  • Skipping foundations to get to the exciting stops. Stop 7 on a weak stop 1 gives you a demo that falls apart.
  • Letting one stop eat the schedule. Stop 3 will tempt you to extend it. Don't. Ship the smaller version.
  • Copying code without checking versions. React, Next.js, the AI SDK and Tailwind have all shifted APIs in recent versions. Always check the docs for what you've installed.
  • Never writing it down. Notes become blog posts, and blog posts become the portfolio.

If you can't do 11 full weeks

Keep all seven stops but shrink the scope inside each:

If you have... Do this
About 5 hours/week Do one mini-project per stop, skip Storybook and i18n, and extend the schedule into January
About 10 hours/week Follow the plan, but cut stop 4's live updates and stop 7's MCP experiment
Full-time availability Follow the plan as written, and add a second project at stops 3 and 5

A plan you finish at 70% beats one you abandon in week three.

Key takeaways

  • A roadmap is only useful if every stop ends with something shipped.
  • Learn React 19's model (actions, use(), the compiler) before layering a framework on top.
  • Treat Server Functions like public endpoints: authenticate and validate inside them.
  • Separate server state, client state and form state, and use the right tool for each.
  • Accessibility, tests and CI are part of building the thing, not a final polish step.
  • AI features are mostly a UX and safety problem. Design the failure states first.

What would you change in this plan? If you've been through some of these stops, which one took longer than expected, and what would you cut or add? And if you're starting it this week, tell me which stop you're most worried about. I'd like to hear how it goes.

articles.body_html:
At AnyPCBA, every board goes through a "health check" before it leaves the factory.

This isn't a single step—it's a chain of inspections: AOI, X-Ray, ICT, and FCT. Each one answers the same question: is this board safe to ship?

But many engineers have a fuzzy understanding of this chain. They know the factory "tests it," but not exactly what's tested, what can be caught, and what can't.

This article breaks down the inspection chain, layer by layer: what each test does, what it can catch, and what it can't.

Layer 1: AOI—Visible Defects Don't Stand a Chance

AOI (Automated Optical Inspection) is the first layer of the chain.

The principle is simple: high-resolution cameras capture the PCB surface and compare it against a "golden reference" image to find differences. It inspects visible solder joints and components.

What AOI can catch:

  • Missing or misaligned components: a component that wasn't placed, or placed incorrectly
  • Solder bridges: two pins that shouldn't be connected, connected by solder
  • Insufficient solder or cold joints: weak or insufficient solder joints
  • Tombstoning: a component standing on one end
  • Polarity errors: diodes, capacitors, or ICs placed in the wrong orientation

AOI is fast and high-coverage, well-suited for high-volume inspection. But its limitation is obvious: it can only see the surface.

For BGA and QFN packages, where the solder joints are hidden beneath the package body, AOI is helpless. The joints are under the chip—the camera can't see them.

Layer 2: X-Ray—Seeing Through the Joints
X-Ray inspection exists to solve AOI's blind spot.

X-Ray uses the penetrating power of X-rays to "see through" BGA bottoms, QFN bottoms, and through-hole interiors. It inspects solder joint quality hidden beneath packages.

What X-Ray can catch:

  • BGA voiding: bubbles inside solder balls, affecting mechanical strength and thermal conductivity
  • Solder ball bridging: adjacent balls under a BGA connected together
  • Missing or shifted solder balls: balls that should be there but aren't, or are misaligned
  • Poor via filling: incomplete fill inside vias, affecting reliability
  • QFN bottom joint defects: poor soldering on the thermal pad under the chip

X-Ray's limitation: it can see the "shape" of a solder joint, but it's hard to directly judge "strength" and "electrical performance." A joint that looks normal may actually be a cold joint.

Layer 3: ICT—Checking Electrical Connections

ICT (In-Circuit Test) uses probes to contact test points on the board and measure electrical parameters point by point.

It checks circuit connection integrity and component electrical performance.

What ICT can catch:

  • Opens: connections that should exist but don't
  • Shorts: connections that shouldn't exist but do
  • Component value deviation: actual resistance or capacitance outside spec
  • Component orientation errors: polarized components placed backwards
  • Missing components: components that should be installed but aren't

ICT's core metric is "coverage." Ideally, every electrical net should have a test point. But in reality, high-density boards have limited test point space, and coverage often falls short of 100%. Insufficient test point coverage means some defects may slip through.

Layer 4: FCT—Verifying Function

FCT (Functional Circuit Test) is the last layer—and the closest to "real-world use."

It powers up the board, simulates actual operating conditions, and verifies whether the board functions correctly.

What FCT can catch:

  • Functional abnormalities: a functional module that doesn't work
  • Performance below spec: excessive output noise, insufficient response speed
  • Timing issues: power-up sequencing or signal timing that doesn't meet requirements
  • Boundary condition failures: abnormal operation under extreme temperature or voltage

FCT's key lies in test case design. The more comprehensive the test cases, the more potential problems are caught. If test cases only cover "normal operating conditions," boundary condition issues will be missed.

One Chain, Different Roles, None Optional

Looking at all four inspections together, their roles are clear:


No single inspection is universal. AOI can't see BGA bottoms. X-Ray can't see electrical performance. ICT can't see functional behavior. FCT can't see long-term reliability.

That's why the chain must be complete. Each inspection covers the blind spot of the one before it.

What This Means for Hardware Engineers

1. Test coverage determines recall rate. If you only do AOI, BGA-related defects will slip through. If you only do ICT, functional abnormalities will slip through.

2. Test point design must happen at the design stage. ICT coverage depends on test point accessibility. If test points aren't reachable, even the best ICT equipment is useless.

3. FCT test cases must cover boundary conditions. Testing only "normal operating conditions" isn't enough. Temperature boundaries, voltage boundaries, and timing boundaries are all potential failure points.

4. Understand the boundaries of each inspection. Don't expect any single inspection to "handle everything." The value of the chain lies precisely in each inspection knowing what it can't see.

At AnyPCBA, our inspection chain covers AOI, X-Ray, ICT, and FCT, serving small-to-medium volume PCB and PCBA projects from 5 to 5000 pieces.

Specifically, what we can support includes:

  • Full AOI inspection: every board goes through automated optical inspection before shipment, checking component placement, solder joint quality, and polarity
  • X-Ray inspection: for BGA, QFN, and other hidden-joint packages, providing void rate, bridging, and offset detection
  • ICT testing: based on the customer's test point design, providing in-circuit test fixtures and test programs
  • FCT functional testing: working with customers to define test cases covering normal operating conditions and boundary conditions
  • Test point accessibility review: checking test point layout during DFM review, catching coverage gaps early
  • Test fixture design and fabrication: for small-to-medium volume projects, providing fast, low-cost test fixture solutions

Our manufacturing capabilities cover 2–64 layers, including HDI, rigid-flex, and high-frequency hybrid. We hold ISO 13485 (medical) and IATF 16949 (automotive) certifications. If you're working on a PCB or PCBA project that needs a complete inspection chain, contact us through our website.

What defects have slipped through inspection in your projects? Share your experience in the comments.
